blocks.text: A newborn is delivered after a difficult shoulder delivery. Her right arm lies limply at her side, rotated inwards, elbow straight, palm facing backwards, yet she can still grip your finger. Knowing exactly which nerve roots were stretched explains this posture, and the brachial plexus is the map that lets you do it.

blocks.markdown: The **brachial plexus** is a network of nerves formed from the **anterior (ventral) rami** of spinal nerves **C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1**. It leaves the neck between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, passes over the first rib behind the clavicle, and enters the axilla, where it surrounds the axillary artery. Its job is to sort the fibres from five spinal levels into the named nerves that supply the shoulder girdle and the whole upper limb. Rather than memorising every branch, learn the five-part scheme and let the branches hang from it.

blocks.title: The five levels of organisation
blocks.text: Going from proximal to distal: five ROOTS (C5-T1) join to form three TRUNKS (upper, middle, lower); each trunk splits into an ANTERIOR and a POSTERIOR DIVISION (six divisions in all); the divisions regroup into three CORDS named by their relation to the axillary artery (lateral, medial, posterior); the cords give rise to the terminal BRANCHES. A common memory aid is: Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches.

blocks.markdown: **Roots to trunks.** C5 and C6 unite to form the **upper trunk**; C7 continues alone as the **middle trunk**; C8 and T1 unite to form the **lower trunk**. These three trunks lie in the posterior triangle of the neck, above the clavicle (the 'supraclavicular' part). **Divisions** are short and lie behind the clavicle. Every trunk divides into an anterior division, which supplies the flexor (anterior) compartments of the limb, and a posterior division, which supplies the extensor (posterior) compartments.

rows: Anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks
Musculocutaneous nerve; lateral root of the median nerve; lateral pectoral nerve
Anterior division of the lower trunk
Ulnar nerve; medial root of the median nerve; medial pectoral nerve; medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm
Posterior divisions of all three trunks
Axillary nerve; radial nerve; upper and lower subscapular nerves; thoracodorsal nerve
blocks.caption: The three cords of the brachial plexus. The median nerve is formed by the union of a lateral and a medial root.

blocks.title: Why the cords are named as they are
blocks.text: The cords are named for their position relative to the second part of the axillary artery (the part behind pectoralis minor): lateral, medial and posterior. They are not named for the trunks that feed them. The posterior cord is the only one that receives all three posterior divisions, so it carries fibres from every root, C5 to T1.

blocks.title: Tracing the median nerve through the plexus
blocks.prompt: Starting at the roots, trace how fibres reach the median nerve and explain why it is not called a lateral or medial cord nerve.

steps.text: The median nerve supplies flexor muscles, so its fibres come from anterior divisions. Anterior divisions of the upper trunk (C5, C6) and middle trunk (C7) form the lateral cord.
The lateral cord gives off the lateral root of the median nerve, which carries mainly C6 and C7 fibres.
The anterior division of the lower trunk (C8, T1) forms the medial cord, which gives off the medial root of the median nerve.
The lateral and medial roots join in front of (or lateral to) the axillary artery to form the median nerve, which therefore carries fibres from roots C6 to T1.

blocks.answer: The median nerve is formed by a lateral root (from the lateral cord, C6-C7) and a medial root (from the medial cord, C8-T1), so it receives fibres from both cords and has no single-cord label.

blocks.markdown: **Branches from the roots and trunks.** Not all branches come from the cords. The **dorsal scapular nerve** (C5) arises from the root and supplies the rhomboids. The **long thoracic nerve** (C5, C6, C7) arises from the roots and runs down the lateral chest wall to serve serratus anterior. From the upper trunk come the **suprascapular nerve** (C5, C6; supraspinatus and infraspinatus) and the nerve to subclavius. Because these branches leave proximal to the cords, they are sometimes called the 'supraclavicular' branches.

rows: Flexors of the arm (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis)
Deltoid and teres minor; skin over the lower deltoid
All extensors of arm and forearm
Most forearm flexors and thenar muscles
Flexor carpi ulnaris, ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, most intrinsic hand muscles
blocks.caption: Terminal branches of the plexus, their cords and spinal levels. Small variations between textbooks exist; the dominant levels are shown.

blocks.title: Which roots does an injury of the axillary nerve implicate?
blocks.prompt: A patient has weak shoulder abduction after a humeral neck fracture, with numb skin over the lower deltoid. Using the plexus scheme, which cord and which spinal levels are involved?

steps.text: Deltoid is an extensor-compartment type muscle (it lies behind the surgical neck of humerus), so its nerve arises from a posterior division.
Posterior divisions form the posterior cord, which gives rise to the axillary nerve.
The axillary nerve carries fibres from the upper trunk, that is, from roots C5 and C6.

blocks.answer: The axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord and carries C5 and C6 fibres.

blocks.markdown: **Clinical application: plexus injuries.** The plexus is most often damaged by traction. Which part is injured depends on the direction of force, and the roots involved predict the picture. An injury to the upper trunk (roots **C5 and C6**) is **Erb palsy** (Erb-Duchenne palsy). Force that widens the angle between the neck and the shoulder, such as a difficult birth with shoulder dystocia or a fall onto the shoulder, stretches the upper trunk. The paralysed muscles include deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis, so the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated: the 'waiter's tip' posture. Sensation is lost over the lateral arm and forearm. A lesion of the lower trunk (roots **C8 and T1**) is **Klumpke palsy**. It follows excessive upward (hyperabduction) traction on the arm, for example grasping a branch while falling or a breech delivery with the arm pulled. The small muscles of the hand supplied by C8 and T1 are weak, giving a claw hand, with sensory loss along the medial forearm and ulnar border of the hand. Because T1 also gives sympathetic fibres to the head via the sympathetic chain, a severe lesion may be accompanied by Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on the same side).

rows: Widening of the neck-shoulder angle (shoulder dystocia, fall on shoulder)
Hyperabduction traction (grasping a branch, breech delivery)
Waiter's tip: adducted, medially rotated, extended elbow, pronated forearm
Medial forearm and ulnar border of hand
Horner syndrome if T1 sympathetic fibres are involved
blocks.caption: Comparing the two classic traction injuries of the brachial plexus.

items: Roots C5-T1 give 3 trunks, 6 divisions and 3 cords.
Anterior divisions supply flexors; posterior divisions supply extensors.
Lateral cord: C5-C7. Medial cord: C8, T1. Posterior cord: C5-T1.
Dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves come off the roots; suprascapular comes off the upper trunk.
Upper trunk injury is Erb palsy; lower trunk injury is Klumpke palsy.

blocks.title: Roots versus nerves
blocks.text: Do not confuse the level at which a structure is injured with its spinal level of origin. A deficit of C8 and T1 function after a plexus injury points to the lower trunk, but the same muscles are also supplied by the ulnar nerve, so a lesion at the elbow gives a similar hand weakness. Always add the pattern of sensory loss and the muscles outside the hand to localise the lesion.

points: The brachial plexus is formed from the anterior rami of C5 to T1, arranged as roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches.
The cords are lateral (C5-C7), medial (C8-T1) and posterior (C5-T1); the median nerve has a root from each of the lateral and medial cords.
Erb palsy damages the upper trunk (C5, C6) and gives the waiter's tip posture; Klumpke palsy damages the lower trunk (C8, T1) and gives a claw hand, sometimes with Horner syndrome.

questions.stem: Which spinal nerve roots unite to form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus?

distractorRationale.b: C6 and C7 do not form a trunk; C7 continues alone as the middle trunk.
distractorRationale.c: C7 alone forms the middle trunk, not the upper trunk.
distractorRationale.d: C8 and T1 form the lower trunk.

questions.explanation: The upper trunk is formed by the union of the anterior rami of C5 and C6. C7 continues as the middle trunk and C8 with T1 form the lower trunk, giving three trunks from five roots.

questions.stem: The posterior cord of the brachial plexus is formed by which of the following?

options.text: Anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks
The anterior division of the lower trunk
The posterior divisions of all three trunks
The posterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks only

questions.correctOptionText: The posterior divisions of all three trunks

distractorRationale.a: These anterior divisions form the lateral cord.
distractorRationale.d: The lower trunk also contributes a posterior division, so all three trunks are included.

questions.explanation: All three posterior divisions join to form the posterior cord, which is why it carries fibres from C5 to T1 and gives the axillary and radial nerves. The anterior divisions form the lateral and medial cords instead.

questions.stem: Which nerve arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus?

distractorRationale.a: The axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord.
distractorRationale.c: The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord.
distractorRationale.d: The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord.

questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve is a terminal branch of the lateral cord (C5-C7) and supplies the flexors of the arm. The lateral cord also gives the lateral pectoral nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.

questions.stem: Which pair of spinal levels is the dominant contribution to the axillary nerve?

distractorRationale.b: C6-C7 is closer to the lateral root of the median nerve, not the axillary nerve.
distractorRationale.c: C7-C8 fibres run mainly in the radial nerve and middle trunk.
distractorRationale.d: C8 and T1 supply the ulnar nerve and small hand muscles.

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve is a branch of the posterior cord carrying fibres from the upper trunk, i.e. C5 and C6. This is why an upper trunk (Erb) lesion weakens deltoid in addition to the elbow flexors.

questions.stem: A newborn after a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia has the right arm held adducted and medially rotated, the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. Grip is preserved. Which roots are most likely injured?

distractorRationale.b: An isolated C7 lesion would not produce this classic posture.
distractorRationale.c: C8-T1 injury would cause a weak grip and claw hand, which is the opposite of the preserved grip here.
distractorRationale.d: T1 alone supplies the small hand muscles and sympathetic fibres; hand function is preserved here.

questions.explanation: The waiter's tip posture with preserved hand function is Erb palsy, an injury to the upper trunk (C5, C6). Deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis lose their supply while the C8-T1 hand muscles remain intact.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man falls from a ladder and grabs a branch, suffering a hyperabduction traction injury. He has a claw hand with sensory loss on the medial forearm, and a small drooping eyelid with a smaller pupil on the same side. Which statement best explains the findings?

options.text: Lower trunk (C8, T1) injury with involvement of T1 sympathetic fibres
Isolated radial nerve injury at the humeral shaft

questions.correctOptionText: Lower trunk (C8, T1) injury with involvement of T1 sympathetic fibres

distractorRationale.b: Upper trunk injury produces shoulder and elbow weakness, not claw hand.
distractorRationale.c: Radial nerve injury at the humeral shaft causes wrist drop and does not explain Horner syndrome.
distractorRationale.d: A lateral cord lesion affects musculocutaneous function and the lateral root of median, not the intrinsic hand muscles or medial forearm.

questions.explanation: Hyperabduction stretches the lower trunk, causing Klumpke palsy with claw hand and medial forearm numbness. Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis) arises because T1 provides the preganglionic sympathetic supply to the head, which is also damaged.

questions.stem: True or false: the long thoracic nerve arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus.

distractorRationale.a: The long thoracic nerve arises directly from the roots, before the cords form.

questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) comes off the roots of the plexus and descends on the lateral chest wall to supply serratus anterior. Only branches distal to the divisions, such as the musculocutaneous nerve, arise from the cords.

questions.stem: Which statement about the median nerve and its origin in the plexus is correct?

options.text: It arises from the posterior cord and carries fibres from C5 to T1
It is formed by lateral and medial roots from the lateral and medial cords
It arises entirely from the medial cord (C8, T1)
It arises from the upper trunk (C5, C6)

questions.correctOptionText: It is formed by lateral and medial roots from the lateral and medial cords

distractorRationale.a: This describes the radial nerve, which comes from the posterior cord.
distractorRationale.c: Only the medial root comes from the medial cord; the lateral root comes from the lateral cord.
distractorRationale.d: The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius, not the median nerve.

questions.explanation: The median nerve is unusual because it receives a lateral root (from the lateral cord, mainly C6-C7) and a medial root (from the medial cord, C8-T1) that unite around the axillary artery. This is why the median nerve carries fibres from C6 to T1.

questions.stem: Describe the organisation of the brachial plexus from roots to cords, stating the spinal levels contributed to each trunk and the divisions that form each cord.
markingGuide: Roots are the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1.
Upper trunk = C5 and C6; middle trunk = C7; lower trunk = C8 and T1.
Each trunk divides into an anterior and a posterior division (six divisions).
Lateral cord = anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks.
Medial cord = anterior division of the lower trunk.
Posterior cord = posterior divisions of all three trunks.
Cords are named by their relation to the axillary artery.
questions.explanation: The plexus follows the sequence roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches, and each step has a rule that can be recalled rather than memorised. Anterior divisions serve flexor compartments and posterior divisions serve extensor compartments, which explains which cord gives which nerve.

questions.stem: A baby has a right brachial plexus injury at birth. Compare Erb palsy and Klumpke palsy in terms of the roots involved, the muscles paralysed and the resulting posture of the limb, and explain why Horner syndrome may accompany one of them.
markingGuide: Erb palsy involves the upper trunk, roots C5 and C6.
Erb palsy paralyses deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis, giving the waiter's tip posture (adducted, medially rotated, extended elbow, pronated forearm).
Klumpke palsy involves the lower trunk, roots C8 and T1.
Klumpke palsy paralyses the intrinsic hand muscles, giving a claw hand.
Horner syndrome may accompany Klumpke palsy because T1 gives the preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head.
Mechanism: Erb by widening of the neck-shoulder angle; Klumpke by hyperabduction traction.
questions.explanation: Linking each palsy to its trunk lets you predict the paralysed muscles and posture from the roots alone. Horner syndrome occurs with Klumpke palsy because the lowest root (T1) also carries sympathetic fibres that are damaged with the lower trunk.
